title: Given a string s and a pattern p, find the smallest substring of s that contains all the characters of p including their required counts, returning an empty result if none exists. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Minimum Window Substring (Smallest Window Containing All Required Characters)

s1_definition.profdef: The minimum window substring problem asks for the shortest substring of a source string that contains every character of a required pattern with at least the pattern's multiplicity. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window plus a frequency map of the pattern and a matched counter: the right pointer expands the window until all required characters are satisfied, then the left pointer contracts the window as far as possible while it still satisfies the requirement, recording the smallest satisfying window. It runs in linear time relative to the source length.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a compliance officer must assemble a complete KYC document packet for Rajesh, needing specific documents in specific quantities, say two address proofs and one identity proof. The documents arrive in a long arrival stream in random order. The officer wants the shortest continuous stretch of the arrival stream that already contains a complete valid packet. They slide a window: expand on the right until the packet is complete, then trim on the left while it stays complete, remembering the shortest complete stretch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand right until all required characters are satisfied, then shrink left while still satisfied, recording the smallest complete window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The minimum window substring problem asks for the shortest substring of a source string that contains every character of a required pattern with at least the pattern's multiplicity. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window plus a frequency map of the pattern and a matched counter: the right pointer expands the window until all required characters are satisfied, then the left pointer contracts the window as far as possible while it still satisfies the requirement, recording the smallest satisfying window. It runs in linear time relative to the source length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a compliance officer must assemble a complete KYC document packet for Rajesh, needing specific documents in specific quantities, say two address proofs and one identity proof. The documents arrive in a long arrival stream in random order. The officer wants the shortest continuous stretch of the arrival stream that already contains a complete valid packet. They slide a window: expand on the right until the packet is complete, then trim on the left while it stays complete, remembering the shortest complete stretch.

**One line to remember:** Expand right until all required characters are satisfied, then shrink left while still satisfied, recording the smallest complete window.

sections.s2_technical:
We first build a frequency map of the pattern, counting how many of each character the pattern requires, for example `need.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)` for each character. We also compute how many distinct requirements must be satisfied, which is the number of keys in that map, and we keep a counter called `formed` for how many of those requirements are currently fully met inside the window. A separate window frequency map tracks counts of the relevant characters currently inside the window.

The right pointer expands the window one character at a time. When it adds a character that the pattern needs, we increment that character's count in the window map, and if the window count for that character now exactly equals the required count, we increment `formed`, meaning one more requirement is fully satisfied. The window is complete when `formed` equals the number of distinct requirements. For example, after adding a needed character we write `if (windowCount.get(c).intValue() == need.get(c).intValue()) formed++;`.

Once the window is complete, we enter a shrink phase. While `formed` still equals the number of requirements, the window is valid, so we record its length if it is the smallest so far, then we remove the leftmost character: we decrement its window count, and if the character was a required one and its window count now drops below the required count, we decrement `formed` because that requirement is no longer satisfied, and we advance the left pointer. The senior-level nuance is that we track the best window's start index and length separately so we can slice it out at the end rather than storing substrings during the scan, which avoids repeated allocation.

The time complexity is linear in the length of the source, O(s + p), because each character is added once and removed once and all map operations are constant time for a bounded alphabet. The space complexity is O(p) for the pattern's requirement map plus the window map, bounded by the alphabet size. This dual-map plus matched-counter technique is the canonical pattern for all contains-all-required-characters window problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the onboarding compliance system ingests a chronological arrival stream of document-type codes for a customer, where each letter represents a document that arrived, such as A for address proof, I for identity proof, P for photograph. A valid KYC packet requires specific documents in specific quantities. Compliance wants the shortest continuous stretch of the arrival stream that already contains one complete valid packet, because that identifies the earliest moment the customer became fully compliant and lets the system auto-approve without waiting for the whole stream. This is exactly the minimum window substring problem.

Problem 2 — Checking every start and end position by brute force is quadratic and too slow for the high volume of concurrent onboarding streams the bank handles. The dual-map sliding window with a matched counter gives a single linear pass per stream, which keeps onboarding real-time.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `KycPacketMatcher` service with a `smallestCompletePacket` method implementing the window, and a runnable `MinWindowSubstringDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's arrival stream against a required packet, logging each shrink at fine level and the final smallest window at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's stream "APAIAPI" with required "AAI", which needs two A and one I. The need map is A to 2 and I to 1, so there are two distinct requirements. We keep a window map, a formed counter at 0, a left boundary at 0, and a best length of a large sentinel.

Step 1: Right at index 0, character A. A is needed, window A becomes 1, which is less than 2, so formed stays 0.

Step 2: Right at index 1, character P. P is not needed, nothing changes.

Step 3: Right at index 2, character A. Window A becomes 2, which equals the required 2, so formed becomes 1.

Step 4: Right at index 3, character I. Window I becomes 1, which equals required 1, so formed becomes 2, matching the two requirements. The window from index 0 to 3, "APAI", is complete, length 4, best becomes 4. Shrink: left character at 0 is A, window A drops to 1, which is below required 2, so formed drops to 1, left moves to 1. Window no longer complete, stop shrinking.

Step 5: Right at index 4, character A. Window A becomes 2 again, equals required 2, formed becomes 2. The window from index 1 to 4, "PAIA", is complete, length 4, best stays 4. Shrink: left character at 1 is P, not needed, left moves to 2. Still complete, window index 2 to 4, "AIA", length 3, best becomes 3. Shrink: left character at 2 is A, window A drops to 1, below required, formed drops to 1, left moves to 3. Stop.

Step 6: Right at index 5, character P, not needed.

Step 7: Right at index 6, character I. Window I becomes 2 but we only need 1; formed stays 1 since the count was already at or above the requirement. Window never reaches formed equal 2 again because A count is only 1.

The smallest complete packet is "AIA" at indices 2 to 4, length 3, containing two address proofs and one identity proof.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: stream "APAIAPI", required "AAI" (need A:2, I:1)
    │
    ▼
  KycPacketMatcher.smallestCompletePacket()
    │ need{A:2,I:1} reqs=2, window={}, formed=0, left=0, best=∞
    │
    ├─ r=0 'A' winA1  formed0
    ├─ r=1 'P' (skip)
    ├─ r=2 'A' winA2=need formed1
    ├─ r=3 'I' winI1=need formed2 complete "APAI" best4
    │      shrink: drop A@0 winA1<need formed1 left=1
    └─ r=4 'A' winA2 formed2 "PAIA" best4
           shrink: P@1 skip left=2 → "AIA" best3
           shrink: A@2 winA1<need formed1 left=3
    │
    ▼
  Output: "AIA"  (earliest complete KYC packet, length 3)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The minimum window substring problem asks for the shortest substring of a source string that contains every character of a required pattern, including the pattern's required counts, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window in time linear in the source length. I first build a frequency map of what the pattern requires and count the number of distinct requirements. Then I expand a right pointer across the source, maintaining a window frequency map and a matched counter that increases each time a required character's count in the window reaches its required amount. When the matched counter equals the number of requirements, the window is complete.

Once complete, I shrink from the left as far as the window stays complete, recording the smallest complete window's start and length as I go, and decrementing the matched counter the moment removing a character drops a requirement below its needed count. I track the best window by its start index and length rather than copying substrings during the scan, so I allocate the result only once at the end. The whole thing is linear because each character is added once and removed once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the onboarding compliance system. We ingested a chronological arrival stream of document-type codes for each customer, and a valid KYC packet required specific documents in specific quantities. We computed the shortest continuous stretch of the arrival stream that already contained a complete valid packet, because that pinpointed the earliest moment the customer became fully compliant and let the system auto-approve immediately instead of waiting for the whole stream. The linear window kept onboarding effectively real-time across many concurrent streams.

The senior-level point I make is that the dual-map plus matched-counter technique is the canonical template for every contains-all-required-characters window problem, and the subtle part is updating the matched counter only on the exact crossing of the required count, both when expanding and when shrinking, because off-by-one there is the classic bug. I also mention that for a bounded alphabet I would switch the maps to fixed integer arrays for speed, and that tracking the best by start and length avoids repeated substring allocation, which matters when the source streams are long. That combination of a clean template and an allocation-aware implementation is what an interviewer wants to hear.
